definitions.definition: A part of the brain just behind your forehead that helps you feel emotions when making decisions, especially about right and wrong.
definitions.example: Like a warning light on a car dashboard that makes you feel something is wrong before you think about it.

definitions.definition: Body signals like a tight chest or queasy stomach that tag choices with a feeling before your brain thinks them through.
definitions.example: Getting a bad feeling in your gut when you're about to do something risky, even if you can't explain why.

definitions.definition: The process of deciding whether something is right or wrong.
definitions.example: When you see someone drop their wallet and you instantly think it's wrong to keep it.

definitions.definition: Babies who are too young to talk or understand language.
definitions.example: A six-month-old who can't say any words yet.

definitions.definition: The study of people and their customs across many different societies around the world.
definitions.example: Comparing how families celebrate birthdays in Japan, Brazil, and Kenya.

definitions.definition: Basic rules about right and wrong that appear in every human society, like caring for others and being fair.
definitions.example: Every culture agrees that hurting a child for no reason is wrong, even if they have different specific rules.

definitions.definition: An inner sense that tells you whether something you did or thought about doing is right or wrong.
definitions.example: Feeling guilty after telling a lie, even if no one finds out.

definitions.definition: A built-in, unchangeable set of rules for judging right and wrong, like software that comes pre-installed on a computer.
definitions.example: A newborn baby already has a basic sense of fairness, just like a phone comes with a clock app you didn't download.

definitions.definition: A mental system that constantly evaluates everything you experience as good or bad, right or wrong, without you choosing to do it.
definitions.example: Like a background app on your phone that runs all the time, checking for updates without you opening it.

definitions.definition: The difference between physical parts of a system (hardware) and the instructions that run on them (software).
definitions.example: Your phone's screen is hardware; the game you play on it is software.

definitions.definition: The basic mental structures and abilities that allow you to think, learn, and understand things.
definitions.example: A baby's brain is like a computer that can only run simple programs at first, then gets more powerful as it grows.

definitions.definition: When something happens that you didn't predict, which scientists measure by how long someone stares at it.
definitions.example: If you see a ball roll uphill, you stare longer because it breaks what you expected.

definitions.definition: Basic categories of right and wrong that show up in every culture, like care, fairness, loyalty, authority, and purity.
definitions.example: Every society has rules about not hurting others (care) and about being honest (fairness).

definitions.definition: The raw, personal feeling of an experience, like the sting of guilt or the warmth of happiness.
definitions.example: The difference between knowing that sugar is sweet and actually tasting the sweetness.

definitions.definition: A quality that appears when simple parts come together in a complex system, but isn't present in any single part.
definitions.example: Wetness is an emergent property of water molecules; no single molecule is wet, but together they are.

definitions.definition: A built-in tool or system that takes readings or makes judgments about something.
definitions.example: A thermometer is a measurement apparatus for temperature; your conscience is a measurement apparatus for right and wrong.

definitions.definition: Being responsible for your actions and having to answer for them, either to yourself, others, or God.
definitions.example: If you break a window, accountability means you have to explain why and make it right.

definitions.definition: A name for God as the one who designed and built the universe and everything in it.
definitions.example: Like an architect who draws up plans for a building, God is the Architect of reality.

definitions.definition: Basic truths that you have to accept without proof in order to build any system of knowledge or belief.
definitions.example: The idea that the world is real and not a dream is an unprovable axiom — you can't prove it, but you have to assume it to live.

definitions.definition: A pattern or framework where all the parts fit together logically and make sense as a whole.
definitions.example: A jigsaw puzzle has a coherent structure when all the pieces connect to form a clear picture.
